title: Core NLP Tasks in Practice
description: Apply the toolkit to real applications: sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, summarization (extractive vs. abstractive), and question answering.

lessons.title: Sentiment Analysis in Practice
lessons.description: Apply everything so far to one of the most common real-world NLP applications.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the sentiment analysis task and the practical challenges that make it harder than it first appears.

sections.title: 🙂🙁 What sentiment analysis does
sections.content: **Sentiment analysis** classifies text according to the emotional tone or opinion it expresses — most commonly positive, negative, or neutral, though finer-grained versions exist too (like a 1-5 star rating, or detecting specific emotions like anger or joy). It's widely used for analyzing product reviews, social media monitoring, and customer feedback at scale.

sections.title: 🛠️ A typical approach
sections.content:
Sentiment analysis is fundamentally a text classification task — everything from earlier modules applies directly. A classical pipeline (TF-IDF + logistic regression) is a very reasonable baseline; embedding-based approaches (averaging word vectors, or using contextual embeddings covered later) often improve on it, especially for more nuanced or complex text.

```python
# Conceptual: same classification pipeline pattern as before
# pipeline.fit(review_texts, sentiment_labels)
# pipeline.predict(["This product exceeded my expectations!"])
# → "positive"
```

sections.title: 😕 Why it's harder than it looks
sections.content:
• **Negation** — "not bad" is actually mildly positive, while "not good" is negative; simple word-counting approaches can struggle with this without n-grams or more context-aware methods
• **Sarcasm** — "oh great, another delay" uses positive words to express negative sentiment — genuinely hard even for advanced models, and often for humans without vocal tone or context
• **Mixed sentiment** — "the food was amazing but the service was terrible" expresses both positive and negative sentiment about different aspects in the same sentence
• **Domain differences** — "unpredictable" is usually negative for a car's brakes, but can be a compliment for a plot twist in a movie review

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating sentiment as a fully solved problem.** Negation, sarcasm, and mixed sentiment remain genuinely challenging even for strong modern models.

**Using a sentiment model trained on one domain (like movie reviews) for a very different domain (like restaurant reviews) without checking performance.** Sentiment-bearing words and their typical meaning can shift meaningfully across domains.

**Reducing every review to a single overall sentiment label when mixed or aspect-specific sentiment matters.** For richer feedback ("food great, service terrible"), aspect-based sentiment analysis — scoring sentiment per topic/aspect separately — is often more useful than one single label.

questions.question: Why is negation (words like 'not') particularly tricky for sentiment analysis?
options: Negation words never actually appear in real text
A word like 'not' can completely flip the sentiment of the words around it, which simple word-counting approaches can struggle to capture correctly
Sentiment analysis ignores individual words entirely
Negation only matters for very long documents
questions.explanation: Since 'not good' and 'good' express opposite sentiment despite sharing a key word, approaches that don't properly account for negation's effect on nearby words can easily misclassify sentiment.

questions.question: Why is sarcasm especially challenging for sentiment analysis models?
options: Sarcastic text never contains any words at all
Sarcasm often uses positive-sounding words to express negative sentiment, which is difficult to detect without broader context or tone
Models are never trained on any negative examples
Sarcasm is easy for models but hard for humans to detect
questions.explanation: Sarcastic statements like 'oh great, another delay' use surface-level positive words to convey the opposite sentiment, which requires understanding context and implication beyond just the literal words used — a genuinely hard problem.

questions.question: Why might a sentiment model trained on movie reviews perform worse on restaurant reviews without adjustment?
options: Sentiment analysis models can only ever be used for one specific domain forever
Sentiment-bearing words and their typical meaning can shift across domains — a word that signals sentiment in one context may not carry the same signal in another
Movie reviews and restaurant reviews always use identical vocabulary
Domain has no actual effect on sentiment analysis performance
questions.explanation: The associations a model learns between words and sentiment are shaped by its training domain — vocabulary and typical usage patterns can differ enough between domains (like movies vs. restaurants) that a model's performance may need to be re-checked or adapted when applied to a new one.

questions.question: What does sentiment analysis classify text according to?
options: Its grammatical structure
The emotional tone or opinion it expresses, like positive, negative, or neutral
The language it's written in
The number of words it contains
questions.explanation: Sentiment analysis assigns a label reflecting the emotional tone or opinion expressed in text, commonly positive, negative, or neutral, though finer-grained versions exist.

questions.question: What is a reasonable baseline pipeline for sentiment analysis, according to the lesson?
options: A random number generator
TF-IDF combined with logistic regression
Stemming alone, with no classifier
Bag-of-words with no machine learning model
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a classical TF-IDF plus logistic regression pipeline as a very reasonable baseline for sentiment analysis, since it's fundamentally a text classification task.

questions.question: What is mixed sentiment, as illustrated by 'the food was amazing but the service was terrible'?
options: A sentence with no sentiment at all
Expressing both positive and negative sentiment about different aspects within the same sentence
A grammatically incorrect sentence
A sentence that is impossible for any model to process
questions.explanation: Mixed sentiment occurs when a single piece of text expresses different sentiments toward different aspects or topics, which a single overall sentiment label may not capture well.

questions.question: Why might 'unpredictable' be negative in one domain but positive in another, per the lesson's example?
options: The word 'unpredictable' has no possible meaning in any domain
The connotation of certain words can shift depending on domain — negative for car brakes, but potentially positive for a movie plot twist
Domain has no effect on word connotation
Sentiment words are always domain-independent
questions.explanation: The same word can carry different sentiment connotations depending on the domain — 'unpredictable' brakes are dangerous, but an 'unpredictable' plot twist can be a compliment.

questions.question: What does the lesson suggest as an alternative to a single overall sentiment label for feedback like 'food great, service terrible'?
options: Ignoring sentiment analysis entirely for such feedback
Aspect-based sentiment analysis, scoring sentiment per topic or aspect separately
Always assigning a neutral label
Removing all sentiment-bearing words from the text first
questions.explanation: For richer, mixed feedback, the lesson suggests aspect-based sentiment analysis, which scores sentiment for each aspect or topic separately rather than forcing one single overall label.

lessons.title: Named Entity Recognition in Practice
lessons.description: Go deeper into how NER actually works and where it gets used in real applications.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe how a modern NER system is typically built and list common real-world applications.

sections.title: 🔁 A quick recap and a deeper look
sections.content:
From module 0: NER identifies and classifies entities (people, organizations, locations, dates, and more) in text. Under the hood, this is usually framed as a **sequence labeling task** — assigning a label to *every* token in a sentence, not just picking out isolated words.

```
Token:  Steve   Jobs    founded  Apple   in    Cupertino
Label:  B-PER   I-PER   O        B-ORG   O     B-LOC
```

This labeling scheme (often called "BIO" tagging) marks the **B**eginning of an entity, tokens **I**nside a multi-token entity, and tokens **O**utside any entity — letting the model correctly handle multi-word entities like "Steve Jobs" as a single unit.

sections.title: 🛠️ How NER models are typically built
sections.content: Modern NER systems are usually trained as sequence models — historically LSTMs, and increasingly the transformer-based models covered in a later course — trained on text where humans have manually labeled every entity span with the correct BIO tags. The model learns to predict these tags for new, unseen text based on patterns like capitalization, surrounding words, and learned knowledge of common entity names.

sections.title: 🌍 Real-world applications
sections.content:
• **Information extraction** — pulling structured facts (people, dates, amounts) out of unstructured documents like contracts or news articles
• **Search and indexing** — letting users search specifically for "articles mentioning this company" rather than just any text match
• **Anonymization / redaction** — automatically finding and removing personal names or sensitive identifiers from documents
• **Customer support routing** — automatically detecting product names or locations mentioned in support tickets to route them appropriately

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming NER works equally well across all domains out of the box.** A model trained on general news text may miss highly specialized entity types (like specific chemical compound names in scientific text) without additional domain-specific training data.

**Not accounting for ambiguous entities.** "Washington" could be a person, a state, or a city — real NER systems rely heavily on context to disambiguate, and can still make mistakes.

**Treating NER output as ground truth without any verification.** For high-stakes uses (like legal document redaction), NER's predictions are a strong starting point, but errors can and do occur — human review is often still warranted for critical applications.

questions.question: How is NER typically framed as a machine learning task?
options: As a document-level classification task, with one label per whole document
As a sequence labeling task, assigning a label to every individual token in a sentence
As an unsupervised clustering task with no labels involved
As a regression task predicting a numeric value
questions.explanation: NER is usually approached as sequence labeling — every token in a sentence gets tagged (like B-PER, I-PER, O) so the model can correctly identify entity boundaries, including multi-word entities.

questions.question: In BIO tagging, what does the 'I' label typically indicate?
options: The token is outside any entity
The token is inside a multi-token entity, continuing one that began with a 'B' tag
The token marks the beginning of a new sentence
The token is a stop word
questions.explanation: The BIO scheme marks the Beginning of an entity with 'B', continues multi-token entities with 'I' (inside), and marks non-entity tokens with 'O' (outside) — this lets the model represent entities that span more than one token, like 'Steve Jobs'.

questions.question: Why might a NER model trained on general news text struggle with a specialized domain like scientific literature?
options: NER models can never be trained on any specific domain
The model may not recognize highly specialized entity types (like specific chemical compounds) it wasn't exposed to during its original training
Scientific text contains no named entities at all
NER performance is unaffected by the domain of the text
questions.explanation: A model's ability to recognize entities depends heavily on what kinds of entities and contexts it saw during training — specialized domains often contain entity types and naming patterns quite different from general news text, requiring domain-specific training data to handle well.

questions.question: What labeling scheme is commonly used for framing NER as sequence labeling?
options: ROUGE scoring
BIO tagging (Beginning, Inside, Outside)
TF-IDF weighting
Cosine similarity scoring
questions.explanation: BIO tagging assigns each token a label marking the Beginning of an entity, tokens Inside a multi-token entity, or tokens Outside any entity.

questions.question: What kinds of models have historically and increasingly been used to build NER systems?
options: Only rule-based dictionaries with no machine learning
Historically LSTMs, and increasingly transformer-based models
Only k-means clustering
Simple linear regression models
questions.explanation: The lesson notes NER systems are usually trained as sequence models — historically LSTMs, and increasingly transformer-based models covered in a later course.

questions.question: What real-world application involves automatically finding and removing personal names from documents?
options: Search and indexing
Anonymization / redaction
Customer support routing
Information extraction for financial reports only
questions.explanation: Anonymization or redaction uses NER to automatically identify and remove personal names or sensitive identifiers from documents.

questions.question: Why might 'Washington' be a challenging entity for a NER system to classify correctly?
options: It can never appear in real text
It could refer to a person, a U.S. state, or a city, requiring context to disambiguate
NER systems automatically ignore all place names
There's no possible ambiguity with 'Washington'
questions.explanation: 'Washington' has multiple possible entity types (person, state, city), so NER systems must rely on surrounding context to determine the correct classification, and can still make mistakes.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend human review of NER output for high-stakes uses like legal redaction?
options: NER output is always perfectly accurate and needs no review
NER predictions are a strong starting point, but errors can occur, so human review is often still warranted for critical applications
Human review is never useful for NER tasks
Legal documents cannot contain any named entities
questions.explanation: Since NER can still make mistakes, especially with ambiguous or unfamiliar entities, human verification remains important for critical, high-stakes applications like legal document redaction.

lessons.title: Text Summarization
lessons.description: Learn the two fundamentally different strategies for automatically condensing long text.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can distinguish extractive from abstractive summarization and explain the tradeoffs between them.

sections.title: ✂️ Extractive summarization: selecting existing sentences
sections.content:
**Extractive summarization** builds a summary by selecting and stitching together a subset of sentences (or phrases) taken directly from the original text — no new sentences are written, existing ones are just chosen and combined.

```
# Original: 10 sentences
# Extractive summary: sentences 1, 4, and 8, selected as most important, presented in order
```

A common approach: score each sentence by importance (using signals like word frequency, position in the document, or similarity to the rest of the text), then select and stitch together the top-scoring sentences.

sections.title: ✍️ Abstractive summarization: generating new text
sections.content:
**Abstractive summarization** generates entirely new sentences that capture the key meaning, potentially using words and phrasing that never appeared in the original text at all — much closer to how a human would actually summarize something in their own words.

This is fundamentally a sequence-to-sequence generation task (recall the encoder-decoder and attention architecture from earlier in this module) — the model reads the full document and generates a new, shorter piece of text expressing its key content.

sections.title: ⚖️ Tradeoffs between the two approaches
sections.content:
• **Extractive** — guaranteed to be grammatically correct and factually consistent with the source (since it only reuses actual source sentences), but can feel choppy or disjointed, and can't paraphrase or truly condense ideas the way a human summary might
• **Abstractive** — can produce a much more natural, human-like, and genuinely concise summary, but risks generating text that's subtly inaccurate or inconsistent with the source (a known and actively studied problem often called **hallucination**) since it's generating new content rather than just selecting existing text

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming abstractive summarization is always strictly better because it "sounds" more human.** Its risk of introducing factual inaccuracies not present in the source is a serious real tradeoff, especially for high-stakes uses like medical or legal document summarization.

**Expecting extractive summaries to read as smoothly as a human-written one.** Since it can only reuse existing sentences verbatim, some choppiness or awkward transitions between selected sentences is a normal, inherent limitation.

**Not verifying an abstractive summary against the source for critical applications.** Given the hallucination risk, some form of verification or spot-checking is often warranted before relying on abstractive summaries for important decisions.

questions.question: What is the key difference between extractive and abstractive summarization?
options: Extractive selects and combines existing sentences from the source text; abstractive generates entirely new sentences that may not appear in the source
They are identical techniques with different names
Abstractive summarization can only be done by humans, never by a model
Extractive summarization always produces longer summaries than abstractive
questions.explanation: Extractive summarization builds a summary purely from selected existing sentences, while abstractive summarization generates new text (potentially with new phrasing) to express the key content — a fundamentally different generation process.

questions.question: What is a key risk specifically associated with abstractive summarization?
options: It can never produce grammatically correct sentences
It can generate text that's subtly inaccurate or inconsistent with the source document, a problem often called hallucination
It always takes longer to compute than extractive summarization
It cannot be used for any real-world application
questions.explanation: Since abstractive summarization generates new content rather than reusing exact source sentences, there's a genuine risk of producing statements that sound plausible but aren't actually accurate or supported by the source text.

questions.question: What is a known limitation of extractive summarization?
options: It always contains factual inaccuracies
Since it can only reuse existing sentences verbatim, the resulting summary can feel choppy or disjointed, and can't truly paraphrase or condense ideas
It requires no source text to work from
It is technically incapable of running on any hardware
questions.explanation: Because extractive summarization is restricted to selecting and combining existing sentences, it can't smooth transitions or genuinely condense and rephrase ideas the way abstractive summarization (or a human) could — this can make its output feel less coherent.

questions.question: How does extractive summarization build its summary?
options: By generating entirely new sentences not present in the source
By selecting and stitching together a subset of existing sentences or phrases from the original text
By translating the source text into another language
By randomly deleting words from the source text
questions.explanation: Extractive summarization builds a summary purely from a selected subset of sentences taken directly from the source, without writing any new sentences.

questions.question: What common signals are used to score sentence importance in extractive summarization?
options: Random number generation only
Word frequency, position in the document, or similarity to the rest of the text
The sentence's exact character count only
The sentence's grammatical tense only
questions.explanation: Sentences are commonly scored using signals like word frequency, their position within the document, and their similarity to the rest of the text, before selecting the top-scoring ones.

questions.question: What architecture does abstractive summarization fundamentally rely on?
options: Bag-of-words vectorization only
Sequence-to-sequence generation, using the encoder-decoder and attention architecture
K-means clustering
Simple stemming and lemmatization
questions.explanation: Abstractive summarization is fundamentally a sequence-to-sequence generation task, using the same encoder-decoder and attention architecture covered earlier in the module.

questions.question: What is a guaranteed property of extractive summaries that abstractive summaries lack?
options: Perfect readability with no choppiness
Grammatical correctness and factual consistency with the source, since it only reuses actual source sentences
The ability to freely paraphrase ideas
Guaranteed shorter length than the original document
questions.explanation: Because extractive summarization only reuses existing sentences verbatim, it's guaranteed to be grammatically correct and factually consistent with the source — a guarantee abstractive summarization, which generates new text, doesn't share.

questions.question: Why is verification against the source especially recommended for abstractive summaries in high-stakes domains?
options: Abstractive summaries are always completely accurate
Abstractive summarization risks hallucination — generating subtly inaccurate or inconsistent content since it creates new text
Verification is never useful for summarization tasks
High-stakes domains never use summarization technology
questions.explanation: Since abstractive summarization generates new content rather than reusing exact source text, there's a real risk of hallucination, making verification especially important for high-stakes applications like medical or legal summarization.

lessons.title: Question Answering Basics
lessons.description: Learn the core task of building systems that answer questions based on a given piece of text.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can distinguish extractive and generative question answering and describe how each approach works.

sections.title: ❓ What question answering (QA) covers
sections.content: **Question answering** systems take a question (and often a source passage of text) and produce an answer. This ranges from simple **reading comprehension** — find the answer within a specific given passage — to open-domain QA, where the system must first find relevant information (potentially from a huge collection of documents) before answering.

sections.title: 📍 Extractive QA: pointing to the answer in the text
sections.content:
**Extractive QA** finds and returns the exact span of text within a given passage that answers the question — rather than generating a new sentence, it identifies where in the source text the answer already exists.

```
Passage: "The Eiffel Tower was completed in 1889 and stands 330 meters tall."
Question: "How tall is the Eiffel Tower?"
Answer (extracted span): "330 meters"
```

This is a natural fit when the answer is a specific fact that literally appears in the source text — the model just needs to correctly locate it.

sections.title: ✍️ Generative QA: composing a new answer
sections.content:
**Generative QA** produces a new, freely composed answer, potentially synthesizing information from multiple parts of a passage (or multiple sources) rather than just pointing to one exact span — much closer to how a person might answer in their own words after reading and understanding the material.

```
Question: "Why is the Eiffel Tower a popular tourist destination?"
# The answer likely isn't one single exact sentence in the source —
# it requires synthesizing several pieces of information together
```

This is a genuinely harder task than extractive QA, and — like abstractive summarization — carries the same hallucination risk, since the model is generating new text rather than just locating an existing answer.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using extractive QA for questions that need synthesis across multiple facts.** If the answer genuinely isn't contained in one contiguous span of text, extractive QA structurally cannot produce it — this calls for a generative approach instead.

**Trusting a generative QA system's confident-sounding answer without verification for important decisions.** As with abstractive summarization, generated answers can sound entirely plausible while still being factually wrong.

**Assuming QA systems have general "understanding" beyond their given source material.** Especially in reading comprehension setups, the system's job is fundamentally to work within the provided passage — not to draw on unstated outside general knowledge, unless it was specifically designed and trained to do so.

questions.question: What does extractive question answering do?
options: It generates an entirely new sentence not found in the source text
It identifies and returns the exact span of text within a given passage that answers the question
It translates the question into another language
It removes the question and returns only the passage
questions.explanation: Extractive QA locates the specific span within the given passage that directly answers the question, rather than composing new text — it's fundamentally about finding where the answer already exists in the source.

questions.question: When is generative QA needed rather than extractive QA?
options: When the answer is a single word or number
When the answer requires synthesizing information from multiple parts of a passage, rather than being a single contiguous span of existing text
Generative QA is never actually needed for any task
When the passage contains no text at all
questions.explanation: If the correct answer can't be found as one exact, contiguous piece of the source text — because it requires combining or reasoning over multiple parts — generative QA's ability to compose a new answer is necessary, since extractive QA can only point to existing spans.

questions.question: Why does generative QA carry a similar risk to abstractive summarization?
options: Both tasks are actually risk-free
Both involve generating new text rather than just extracting existing content, which creates a risk of producing plausible-sounding but factually inaccurate output
Neither task can be evaluated in any way
Generative QA never actually generates any new text
questions.explanation: Since generative QA composes new answers rather than pointing to existing text, it shares the same hallucination risk as abstractive summarization — the output can sound confident and correct while still containing inaccuracies not actually supported by the source.

questions.question: What does reading comprehension QA involve?
options: Answering questions without any given source passage
Finding the answer within a specific given passage
Translating the question into another language
Generating a random answer with no reference to any text
questions.explanation: Reading comprehension is a form of QA where the system finds the answer within a specific, given passage of text.

questions.question: What must the answer be for extractive QA to successfully find it?
options: Any freely composed sentence
An exact span of text that literally exists within the passage
A translation of the passage
A summary of the entire passage
questions.explanation: Extractive QA works by locating an existing contiguous span of text within the passage — it can't produce an answer that isn't literally present in the source.

questions.question: What must generative QA sometimes do that extractive QA cannot?
options: Copy text exactly from a single sentence
Synthesize information from multiple parts of a passage or multiple sources into a new answer
Avoid using any information from the passage
Refuse to answer any question at all
questions.explanation: Generative QA can compose an answer that combines or synthesizes information spread across multiple parts of a passage, which extractive QA — limited to a single existing span — cannot do.

questions.question: What risk does generative QA share with abstractive summarization?
options: Neither approach carries any risk at all
The risk of hallucination — generating plausible-sounding but factually inaccurate content
The risk of being unable to process any text
The risk of only working with numeric data
questions.explanation: Since generative QA composes new text rather than pointing to an existing answer span, it shares the same hallucination risk described for abstractive summarization.

questions.question: According to the lesson, should a QA system be assumed to draw on general outside knowledge beyond its given source material?
options: Yes, always, regardless of design
Not necessarily — especially in reading comprehension setups, the system's job is to work within the provided passage unless specifically designed otherwise
QA systems never use any given passage at all
All QA systems are identical in this regard
questions.explanation: The lesson cautions against assuming a QA system draws on unstated outside knowledge — particularly in reading comprehension setups, it's meant to work within the provided passage unless explicitly built to do more.
